story.headline: US sanctions ICC president
story.summary: The US Treasury sanctioned ICC President Tomoko Akane of Japan and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, the sharpest escalation yet against the court.
story.display_body: The United States sanctioned the president of the International Criminal Court, Japan's Tomoko Akane, and a senior ICC trial lawyer, Senegal's Abdoulaye Seye, on Tuesday 18 August. the sharpest escalation yet in the Trump administration's campaign against The Hague-based court. The US Treasury added both to its sanctions list under the executive order Washington issued against the ICC earlier this year; Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the two had "directly engaged" in ICC efforts to investigate or prosecute officials of governments that have not accepted the court's jurisdiction — the wording points at the court's warrants touching US and Israeli officials, though the administration frames the whole institution as "politicized." Treasury issued a general licence allowing existing dealings with Akane to be wound down by 17 September. Japan's government called the move "very regrettable," a rare public rebuke of Washington from a close G7 ally over one of its own nationals.
story.why: Sanctioning the sitting head of the world's permanent war-crimes court — and a Japanese jurist at that — targets the institution itself rather than a case, and puts a G7 government in the position of protesting sanctions on its own citizen. The ICC's ability to function depends on banks, staff, and states not treating association with its leadership as a legal risk; that is precisely what the designation is designed to create.

story.headline: Israel bombs Syrian air base
story.summary: Israel struck the Abu Duhur air base in Idlib, Syria to stop Turkish troops deploying there, drawing condemnation from Syria and Turkey.
story.display_body: Israel struck the Abu Duhur air base in Syria's northwestern Idlib province early Tuesday 18 August, saying the aim was to stop Turkish forces from deploying there. Israeli state accounts and Syrian state TV described roughly eight strikes on the runway, causing damage but no reported casualties. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said Syria had been "on the verge of breaching" an agreed security "status quo" by letting Turkish troops move in, and that Israel had warned Damascus the deployment would threaten its security. Syria's foreign minister, Asaad al-Shibani, condemned the raid as an "unjustified provocation" and a violation of sovereignty; Turkey's foreign ministry also condemned it, and Qatar, Egypt and Saudi Arabia issued statements against the strikes.
story.why: The strike opens a direct friction point between Israel and Turkey — two US-aligned militaries — over who gets to operate inside post-Assad Syria, and signals Israel intends to police a buffer around its northern frontier by force even against a NATO member's plans.

story.headline: France enacts assisted-dying law
story.summary: Macron promulgated France's assisted-dying law, making medical aid in dying legal for terminally ill adults after the Constitutional Council cleared it.
story.display_body: France's assisted-dying law was promulgated by President Emmanuel Macron and formally took effect on Wednesday 19 August, making medical aid in dying legal for the first time. The step follows the Constitutional Council's ruling on Friday 14 August that found no grounds to strike the text down, which itself followed the National Assembly's final adoption on 15 July after years of debate. Under the law, adults with a "serious and incurable" illness in an advanced or terminal phase, suffering that cannot be relieved, may request assistance to die; access will phase in as implementing decrees follow. It is one of France's most consequential social reforms in a decade.
story.why: France joins the small group of European states with a legal right to die, resolving a debate that has run through French politics for years — and the outcome next door feeds directly into how Switzerland, which already permits assisted suicide, and its neighbours frame their own end-of-life rules.

story.headline: France to expel two Iranian diplomats
story.summary: France announced it will expel two Iranian diplomats in retaliation for the July detention of two French diplomats in Tehran.
story.display_body: France announced on Tuesday 18 August that it will expel two Iranian diplomats. in retaliation for what Paris says was the "deliberate" assault and hours-long detention of two of its own diplomats in Tehran on 19 July. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the "intolerable act would have consequences"; Iran's foreign ministry responded that the two French diplomats would not be allowed to return to Iran. The July incident is entangled with the continued detention of two Iranian graphic-design artists arrested during a cultural meeting with the French officials.

story.headline: Federal Council seeks 970M for air defence
story.summary: The Swiss Federal Council asked parliament for a 970-million-franc supplementary credit to speed up ground-based air-defence procurement.
story.display_body: The Federal Council asked parliament on Wednesday 19 August for a supplementary credit of about 970 million francs to speed up the build-out of Switzerland's air defence, plus a further 100 million for civil protection. The request (a Nachtragskredit — an in-year addition to the approved budget) breaks down as roughly 250 million francs for shorter-range ground-based air defence, 650 million for medium-range systems, 60 million for radar and 10 million for defending against mini-drones. The government says the money is needed for advance payments to lock in delivery slots, arguing that surging global demand has stretched arms-makers' production and lengthened lead times, so manufacturers now want substantial money up front. It cites a "heightened threat situation" as the justification.
story.why: The credit is a concrete measure of how far Switzerland's post-neutrality-debate rearmament has moved from principle to cash — and it commits money before parliament has finished the larger fight over how to fund the army, including the temporary VAT rise the Council has separately proposed.

story.headline: Swiss individual taxation delayed to 2032
story.summary: The Federal Council set 2032 as the entry-into-force date for the switch to individual taxation.
story.display_body: The switch to individual taxation in Switzerland will not take effect until 2032, the Federal Council confirmed on Wednesday 19 August. years later than campaigners had hoped. The reform would tax spouses separately rather than jointly, ending the long-criticised "marriage penalty" under which some two-earner couples pay more than two unmarried earners on the same income; the delayed date reflects the scale of the changeover for cantonal tax authorities and IT systems. The reform still faces a likely referendum.
story.why: For two-income households in Switzerland this is the reform that decides whether marriage carries a tax cost — and a 2032 start means the current joint-taxation rules, and the penalty they can impose, stay in place for years yet.
